\chapter{Veo a María --- The Little A That Guards People}
\label{ch:veo-a-maria}
\hlchaptermodality{239}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can mark the person on the receiving end of a verb.}

I can mark the person on the receiving end of a verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[veo a María]{veo a María — the little a that guards people}

\label{lesson:ES-C62-veo-a-maria}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Veo} — I see. And \emph{a}, which you know as \emph{to}, \emph{towards}.

Watch what happens when what I see is a \textbf{person}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it appears, then vanishes}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{Veo la casa.} & I see the house \\
\emph{Veo} \emph{\textbf{a}} \emph{María.} & I see María \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Nothing in the English moved. In the Spanish, a preposition appeared out of nowhere — and it is not optional. \emph{Veo María} is wrong.

It is not doing its usual job either. Nobody is going \emph{towards} María. The \emph{a} is there purely because the thing being seen is a person.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Remember what happened to \emph{quién}: Latin marked the object of a sentence with an \textbf{ending}, and Spanish threw those endings away. That was cheap for things — a house is unlikely to be seeing anybody — but expensive for people, because with two people in a sentence, word order alone has to carry who did what.

So Spanish grew a replacement. The little \emph{a} marks the person on the \textbf{receiving} end, doing by hand the job the lost ending used to do for free.

Which is why it guards people and ignores houses. The ambiguity it protects against only ever arises with people.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Veo la casa}, then \emph{Veo a María}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When does the little \emph{a} appear? (When the thing on the receiving end is a \textbf{person}.)

And is it optional? (\textbf{No.} \emph{Veo María} is simply wrong.)
\end{tcolorbox}
